hints: Look carefully at what area C represents in the Venn diagram, it is the very centre where amylose, cellulose and glycogen all overlap.
Ask yourself what links the glucose monomers in each polysaccharide, remembering that amylose, cellulose and glycogen are all long glucose chains with straight sections.
walkthrough:
**Read the Venn Diagram**

First, work out what each letter means. It is like a map of shared features.

A is amylose only. D is shared by amylose and cellulose. B is shared by amylose and glycogen. C is the centre shared by all three.

**Recall the Bonds in Each Polysaccharide**

All three are polymers of glucose joined by glycosidic bonds formed by condensation.

Amylose: $\alpha$-glucose joined by 1,4-glycosidic bonds in an unbranched chain. Glycogen: $\alpha$-glucose joined by 1,4-glycosidic bonds with 1,6-glycosidic bonds at branches. Cellulose: $\beta$-glucose joined by 1,4-glycosidic bonds in straight chains.

**Find the Common Bond**

So although one uses $\beta$-glucose and the others use $\alpha$-glucose, all three use 1,4-glycosidic bonds to make their main chains.

That common feature belongs in the centre of the Venn, which is area C.

options.A: This is amylose only, but cellulose and glycogen also contain 1,4-glycosidic bonds, so this area is too narrow.
options.B: This is shared by amylose and glycogen only, but it leaves out cellulose which also has 1,4-glycosidic bonds.
options.C: This is the centre shared by all three, which is correct because amylose, cellulose and glycogen all contain 1,4-glycosidic bonds in their chains.
options.D: This is shared by amylose and cellulose only, but it leaves out glycogen which also has 1,4-glycosidic bonds in its straight sections.
